intl-philippines-bsp-cash-withdrawal-che.headline: Philippines pauses its automatic extra checks on cash withdrawals over 1 million pesos a day until Jan 31, the central bank's memo confirms
intl-philippines-bsp-cash-withdrawal-che.org: Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (the Philippines' central bank)
intl-philippines-bsp-cash-withdrawal-che.what_changed: Major Philippine newspapers reported on Nov 16, 2026 that, in a memorandum, the central bank's policy-making Monetary Board suspended until Jan 31, 2027 the threshold that triggers enhanced due diligence (extra background and transaction checks) on cash transactions above ₱1 million in a banking day. The board approved the step on Nov 12 and it took effect Nov 13. The central bank said the aim is to facilitate legitimate transactions and support the public's cash needs during the holidays. Banks must still apply due diligence and enhanced checks when transactions look unusual or a customer's profile changes, keep monitoring transactions, and file suspicious-transaction reports; cash transactions above ₱500,000 must still be reported to the Anti-Money Laundering Council.
intl-philippines-bsp-cash-withdrawal-che.summary: The central bank began requiring the extra checks in September 2025 for cash withdrawals above ₱500,000 a day (Circular 1218), amid investigations into alleged kickbacks from government flood-control projects. A Feb 6, 2026 memorandum told banks to run the checks once per customer rather than for every withdrawal, and Circular 1230 of Feb 27, 2026 raised the trigger to ₱1 million after banks and businesses said routine payouts such as payroll and loan releases were being caught. The central bank has said the threshold was never an absolute withdrawal limit, since larger withdrawals were allowed after verification, and banks may still set stricter internal limits based on their own risk reviews. We couldn't open the new memorandum itself, but several major outlets quote it and the central bank's statement. The central bank's Memorandum No. M-2026-050, posted on its website, confirms that the Monetary Board approved the pause on Nov 12 (Resolution No. 1086), that it took effect when the memo was issued and that it lasts until Jan 31, 2027. Separately, on Nov 18 the central bank called a viral video claiming banks nationwide would close on Nov 20 false; Meta had taken it down.
intl-philippines-bsp-cash-withdrawal-che.plain: The Philippines paused extra bank checks on very big cash withdrawals, over 1 million pesos a day, until Jan 31. Banks must still check ones that look odd.
intl-philippines-bsp-cash-withdrawal-che.why_it_matters: It's a live example of a government adding checks that can slow large cash withdrawals, then easing them when they got in the way of normal business. Rules like this are often what people have in mind when they talk about withdrawal limits.
intl-philippines-bsp-cash-withdrawal-che.why_it_might_not: It loosens an anti-money-laundering rule rather than adding a limit, it covers only very large cash withdrawals in the Philippines, and the underlying rule calls for checks, not a cap.
intl-philippines-bsp-cash-withdrawal-che.us_link: No direct link. U.S. banks must report cash transactions over $10,000 to the government, a reporting rule rather than a limit, and we found no U.S. proposal to require checks or caps on large cash withdrawals.

irs-1545-BQ82-carf.what_changed: The White House budget office's list of rules under review, dated Nov 16, 2026, still shows the IRS proposed rule 'CARF: U.S. Broker Digital Transaction Reporting' (RIN 1545-BQ82), received Nov 14, 2025. Its text stays confidential until review ends and it is published for public comment.
irs-1545-BQ82-carf.summary: CARF, the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, is a standard from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) under which countries automatically swap information on people's crypto accounts and transactions, much as they already do for bank accounts. By joining, the U.S. would receive data on Americans' crypto accounts held abroad and would send other countries data on their residents' accounts at U.S. firms. A July 2025 White House report urged Treasury to consider such rules without adding reporting on decentralized finance, and the U.S. has said it intends to implement CARF by 2029. It is a tax-reporting step: it would let the government see accounts, not block or limit transactions.
irs-1545-BQ82-carf.plain: The IRS (the U.S. tax agency) wants to join a system where countries share crypto account details, but the plan has waited a year for White House review. It would let the IRS see Americans' crypto abroad, not limit it.
irs-1545-BQ82-carf.why_it_matters: It would give the IRS automatic visibility into crypto Americans hold on foreign platforms, closing one of the last big gaps in cross-border account reporting, and U.S. crypto platforms would report on their foreign customers.
irs-1545-BQ82-carf.why_it_might_not: It's a tax-information exchange like those already in place for foreign bank accounts, and it wouldn't let anyone block, delay or cap a transaction. It has sat at the White House for a year, and its final shape and timing are unknown.

claim-nov17-digital-apocalypse-rumor-202.headline: Viral rumor: a Nov 17 'digital apocalypse' would wipe out bank balances and shut down the internet for up to three months
claim-nov17-digital-apocalypse-rumor-202.org: Social media posts on X, TikTok, Facebook and Instagram
claim-nov17-digital-apocalypse-rumor-202.who: Anonymous and viral social media accounts, starting with an Oct 31 post on X that drew more than 3 million views
claim-nov17-digital-apocalypse-rumor-202.claim: On Nov 17, 2026, hackers or a global blackout would erase bank account balances, shut down ATMs and cut off the internet for up to three months, so people should withdraw their money.
claim-nov17-digital-apocalypse-rumor-202.claimant: Viral social media posts, beginning with an anonymous Oct 31 post on X (more than 3 million views) and spreading through TikTok, Facebook and Instagram videos
claim-nov17-digital-apocalypse-rumor-202.what_changed: Nov 17, 2026 came and went without the predicted wipeout of bank balances or a long blackout, and we found no reports of frozen or erased bank accounts that day; U.S. stock markets traded normally. The only scheduled event was FEMA and the FCC's nationwide Emergency Alert System test on TV and radio at about 2:20 p.m. ET, announced in September, with no alerts sent to phones; FEMA posted on Nov 16 that there would be no blackouts and no secret emergencies. Fact-checkers including Snopes, France 24 and PopFake found no evidence for the claim, and PopFake rated it fake after rechecking late on Nov 17.
claim-nov17-digital-apocalypse-rumor-202.summary: The rumor traced back to an anonymous post that offered no documents or data, then picked up details as it spread across languages, including a claim that a 'Simpsons' episode predicted it. It gained traction after real outages: a widespread email outage on Nov 12, a nationwide flight ground stop on Nov 13 and the Chase software bug on Nov 16 (tracked), which the bank fixed that evening. France 24 reported that some cryptocurrency accounts used the scare to urge people to withdraw their savings and buy crypto. Nothing in the official record pointed to a plan or an attack to wipe out accounts.
claim-nov17-digital-apocalypse-rumor-202.plain: Viral posts said bank accounts would be wiped out on Nov 17. No proof: the day passed with banks working, and the only planned event was a one-minute alert test on TV and radio.

intl-em-stablecoin-ramp-controls-2026-11.headline: Thailand, Nigeria and Brazil apply currency-style limits to stablecoins: Thailand proposes a 5 million baht daily cap per platform, Nigeria requires approval to swap naira for dollar coins, and Brazil bars them in cross-border payment services
intl-em-stablecoin-ramp-controls-2026-11.org: Securities and Exchange Commission of Thailand; Central Bank of Nigeria; Central Bank of Brazil
intl-em-stablecoin-ramp-controls-2026-11.what_changed: Thailand: on Nov 12, 2026, the SEC opened a consultation, closing Nov 26, on draft rules that would cap each customer's stablecoin transfers into and out of their account at a licensed digital asset platform at 5 million baht (about $147,750) a day per platform in each direction, allow transfers only between accounts or wallets belonging to the same person, and require amounts to match the customer's income and financial position. Transfers between a customer's own accounts at SEC-supervised platforms that follow the Travel Rule, market makers and some approved business uses would be exempt, and purely peer-to-peer transfers outside licensed platforms aren't covered. Nigeria: on Nov 5, the Central Bank of Nigeria issued rules, effective immediately, under which swapping naira for a dollar-linked stablecoin needs specific central bank approval and settlement through, or reporting to, an authorized foreign-exchange dealer; cross-border stablecoin transactions are treated as foreign exchange; and peer-to-peer platforms must check that the name and bank verification number (BVN) on the paying naira account match their customer. Brazil: since Oct 1, Resolution BCB 561 has required companies that offer international payment and transfer services (eFX) to settle with their partners abroad only through foreign-exchange transactions or nonresident accounts in reais, expressly barring the use of virtual assets.
intl-em-stablecoin-ramp-controls-2026-11.summary: Each measure is framed as anti-money-laundering or foreign-exchange supervision. Thailand's SEC says the aim is to stop money laundering, cybercrime and the circumvention of rules on international money transfers, and Nigeria's central bank lists keeping its ability to monitor and manage capital flows among its goals; a law-firm guide says Nigeria can also suspend or cap naira-to-stablecoin conversions at any time. Together they move existing currency controls onto the points where stablecoins meet the banking system, after IMF research (tracked) found stablecoin use rises when countries restrict money leaving. Thailand's cap is still a draft; the Nigerian and Brazilian rules are in force. None of this applies in the U.S.
intl-em-stablecoin-ramp-controls-2026-11.plain: Thailand, Nigeria and Brazil are adding limits on stablecoins (digital dollars made by companies). Thailand may cap how much of them each person moves on a platform in a day. These rules apply only there.

quote.text: commensurate with the customer's source of income and financial position

intl-em-stablecoin-ramp-controls-2026-11.us_link: No U.S. counterpart. U.S. stablecoin rules (the GENIUS Act, tracked) require issuers to be able to freeze coins under lawful orders, but no U.S. rule caps stablecoin transfers or requires approval to convert dollars into them.
intl-em-stablecoin-ramp-controls-2026-11.why_it_matters: It shows governments that already manage their currencies moving controls to stablecoin on-ramps, with tools such as daily caps and same-owner-only transfers that could be copied elsewhere.
intl-em-stablecoin-ramp-controls-2026-11.why_it_might_not: These are countries with managed exchange rates and existing currency controls; the U.S. has neither. Thailand's cap is only a draft, and the rules cover licensed platforms, not every wallet.

intl-moldova-fx-liberalization-2026-11.headline: Moldova's eased foreign-exchange rules take effect: residents can send or invest up to 100,000 euros abroad without central bank approval, up from 10,000
intl-moldova-fx-liberalization-2026-11.org: National Bank of Moldova; Parliament of Moldova (Law No. 226)
intl-moldova-fx-liberalization-2026-11.what_changed: On Nov 20, 2026, Law No. 226 amending Moldova's foreign-exchange law took effect, on the date set when it was published in the Official Journal on Oct 20. People and companies in Moldova can now carry out covered foreign-exchange transactions of up to 100,000 euros without authorization from the National Bank of Moldova, up from 10,000 euros, rising to 250,000 euros from Jan 1, 2028. The covered transactions include buying foreign shares, bonds and fund units, lending to or guaranteeing nonresidents, and opening some accounts abroad; residents can also buy foreign securities admitted to trading in Moldova without authorization, whatever the amount. The monthly limit on foreign-currency cash withdrawals abroad with Moldovan bank cards also rises from 10,000 to 100,000 euros per account, and residents who emigrate can open bank accounts abroad without authorization.
intl-moldova-fx-liberalization-2026-11.summary: The central bank says the changes bring Moldova's rules closer to the European Union's free movement of capital as part of its EU integration. Banks will still check the source of funds and the purpose of transactions to prevent money laundering, and the rules on carrying cash across the border don't change. A requirement to notify the central bank of some foreign loans ends on Oct 1, 2027.
intl-moldova-fx-liberalization-2026-11.plain: Since Nov 20, people in Moldova can send or invest up to 100,000 euros abroad without asking the central bank, up from 10,000 euros. This eases limits there.
intl-moldova-fx-liberalization-2026-11.us_link: None. It is an example of a country removing approval requirements on moving money abroad as it aligns with EU rules.
intl-moldova-fx-liberalization-2026-11.why_it_matters: It is a concrete easing of capital controls: a government dropping approval requirements for moving and investing money abroad, the opposite of the trend this monitor watches for.
intl-moldova-fx-liberalization-2026-11.why_it_might_not: Moldova is a small economy outside the EU aligning with EU rules; its choices say little about U.S. policy.

claim-napier-france-capital-controls-202.headline: Financial historian Russell Napier: France will impose capital controls, freezing about $6 trillion of foreign-owned French assets and setting off a global credit crunch
claim-napier-france-capital-controls-202.org: ETF Stream (report of a talk at its ETF Buyer London event)
claim-napier-france-capital-controls-202.who: Russell Napier, financial historian and investment strategist
claim-napier-france-capital-controls-202.claim: France will effectively default on its debt by imposing capital controls that lock up about $6 trillion of French assets owned by foreigners, triggering a global credit crunch.
claim-napier-france-capital-controls-202.claimant: Russell Napier, speaking at ETF Stream's ETF Buyer London event, as reported by ETF Stream on Nov 17, 2026
claim-napier-france-capital-controls-202.what_changed: ETF Stream reported on Nov 17, 2026 that Russell Napier told its ETF Buyer London event the week before that France will respond to its debt problems the way Cyprus (2013) and Greece (2015) did, by imposing capital controls that would lock up roughly $6 trillion of liquid French assets held by foreigners (about $2 trillion of stocks and $4 trillion of debt securities). He said foreign investors hold 56% of French government bonds and, citing IMF data, that U.S. investors are the largest foreign owners of French portfolio assets, at $856 billion. He called the resulting global credit crunch and forced financial repression imminent.
claim-napier-france-capital-controls-202.summary: Parts of the backdrop are real. France's 10-year government bond yield was about 4.85% on Nov 18, roughly 1 percentage point higher than six months earlier, and euro-area countries have used capital controls before: EU law generally bans limits on moving money but allows measures on public-policy or public-security grounds, which Cyprus (2013) and Greece (2015) used. But this is a forecast, not a report of a plan. We found no proposal by France or the EU to limit moving money out of France, Moody's left France's credit rating unchanged on Oct 23, and ETF Stream reported that many in the audience disagreed. The claim is about France, not limits on Americans' own accounts, though U.S. holders of French stocks and bonds would be affected if it happened. Commentary can't raise this monitor's level.
claim-napier-france-capital-controls-202.plain: Financial historian Russell Napier said France will freeze about $6 trillion of French stocks and bonds owned by foreigners. Can't tell yet: it's a guess about the future, and France hasn't proposed limits like that.

quote.text: the imposition of capital controls in France

claim-napier-france-capital-controls-202.why_it_matters: Napier is a widely followed market historian, and the warning ties a real rise in French borrowing costs to past euro-area capital controls. If it happened, U.S. investors, the largest foreign holders of French stocks and bonds by his count, would be affected.
claim-napier-france-capital-controls-202.why_it_might_not: It's one analyst's forecast, not a report of a plan or proposal, and EU law allows such controls only in exceptional circumstances.

intl-romania-cash-cap-raise-2026-11.headline: Romania's parliament votes to raise the daily cap on cash payments by businesses to 50,000 lei, from 5,000 or 10,000 lei
intl-romania-cash-cap-raise-2026-11.org: Parliament of Romania (Chamber of Deputies, the deciding chamber)
intl-romania-cash-cap-raise-2026-11.what_changed: On Nov 18, 2026, Romania's Chamber of Deputies, the deciding chamber for this bill after the Senate had rejected it, passed an amendment to Law No. 70/2015 on cash discipline that sets a single daily cap of 50,000 lei on cash receipts and payments by companies, authorized self-employed people, sole proprietorships, family businesses, liberal professions and associations. It replaces the current caps of 5,000 or 10,000 lei, depending on the type of transaction. The bill came from lawmakers of the AUR party, which said it passed with 173 votes.
intl-romania-cash-cap-raise-2026-11.summary: Under the bill, a business may take in up to 50,000 lei a day in cash from any one person, cash-and-carry wholesale stores get the same limit, and payments from cash advances are capped at 50,000 lei a day per person. Splitting a bill or invoice worth more than 50,000 lei into smaller cash payments stays banned. The bill still needs the president's signature (promulgation) to become law. Separately, from July 10, 2027, an EU-wide anti-money-laundering rule will bar businesses across the EU from accepting or making cash payments above 10,000 euros; member states may set lower limits.
intl-romania-cash-cap-raise-2026-11.plain: Romania's lawmakers voted to let businesses take in or pay up to 50,000 lei in cash a day, up from 5,000 or 10,000 lei. It still needs the president's signature.
intl-romania-cash-cap-raise-2026-11.us_link: None. U.S. businesses may accept cash of any amount but must report cash payments over $10,000; we found no U.S. proposal to cap them.
intl-romania-cash-cap-raise-2026-11.why_it_matters: It is a government loosening a limit on cash payments, the opposite of the cash caps this monitor watches, such as Canada's proposed Bill S-8 and the EU's coming 10,000-euro limit.
intl-romania-cash-cap-raise-2026-11.why_it_might_not: It applies only in Romania, still needs the president's signature, and from July 2027 the EU-wide 10,000-euro limit on business cash payments will also apply there.

intl-imf-cbdc-policy-paper-2026-11.headline: IMF paper says CBDC talks are shifting to central bank money as infrastructure for tokenized finance, including technology to strengthen compliance
intl-imf-cbdc-policy-paper-2026-11.org: International Monetary Fund (Monetary and Capital Markets Department)
intl-imf-cbdc-policy-paper-2026-11.who: IMF staff, in a paper informing the IMF Executive Board
intl-imf-cbdc-policy-paper-2026-11.what_changed: On Nov 17, 2026, the IMF published a policy paper (Policy Paper No. 2026/051, 'Central Bank Digital Currency - Looking Ahead Towards Future Financial Infrastructure') that informs its Executive Board about developments in central bank digital currency (CBDC) and summarizes the fourth and final wave of chapters in its CBDC Virtual Handbook.
intl-imf-cbdc-policy-paper-2026-11.summary: The IMF says policy discussions are shifting from issuing a CBDC to the role of central bank money in increasingly digital, tokenized and interconnected financial systems. The new chapters cover CBDC concepts and design choices, CBDC as financial infrastructure, links with next-generation capital markets, and opportunities to use technology to strengthen compliance. The paper guides member countries; it doesn't set rules or limits, and its published summary doesn't mention holding limits or capital flow measures. The Handbook is funded by the government of Japan.
intl-imf-cbdc-policy-paper-2026-11.plain: The IMF (a group of 190 countries that lends to governments) wrote about digital money made by central banks. It looks at design and at using tech to help follow rules. It sets no limits.

intl-imf-cbdc-policy-paper-2026-11.why_it_matters: IMF guidance shapes how many central banks design digital money, and its focus on technology to strengthen compliance points toward rule checks built into payment systems, the kind of feature this monitor watches.
intl-imf-cbdc-policy-paper-2026-11.why_it_might_not: It's a staff summary of handbook chapters for the IMF Board, not a rule or a recommendation for the U.S., and U.S. law currently bars a Fed retail CBDC.

raise_level_triggers: A cap on, or a government approval requirement for, individual transfers abroad, beyond sanctions and national-security investment screening.
H.R. 8995, or any similar bill raising the remittance tax or extending it to bank- and card-funded transfers, getting a hearing, a markup or a ride on a must-pass bill.

FinCEN extending cross-border reporting orders to more regions, lowering thresholds, renewing them repeatedly or making them permanent; a new proposal to lower the $3,000 record-keeping and travel-rule threshold for transfers abroad; or a rule implementing FATF's payment-transparency standard that adds source-of-funds or approval steps for ordinary transfers abroad.

Any regulator discussing temporary limits on deposit withdrawals or bank holidays, bringing back money-fund redemption gates, or extending liquidity fees to government or retail funds, or officials applying terms like 'temporary liquidity restrictions' or 'capital flow management' to U.S. deposits, stablecoins or money funds.

FDIC provisional holds being used at a large bank failure, a cluster of failures in a short period, or several large banks adding unexplained withdrawal or wire limits (confirmed by banks or regulators, not social media).

Final stablecoin rules allowing freezes without a specific lawful order, extending freeze duties to all secondary-market holders, restricting self-hosted wallets, or a mandatory (not voluntary) hold regime for crypto withdrawals.
Rules that let anyone other than the payer and payee, such as a government or bank acting without a court order, set or override conditions on tokenized deposits.

Emergency powers (IEEPA, the new Russia/Iran sanctions law or the Defense Production Act) used against U.S. persons' general transactions, gold or foreign currency, or lifting the EO 14436 waivers with restrictions on U.S. persons.
Requirements for retirement accounts, money funds or banks to hold set shares of Treasury debt, or new limits on retirement withdrawals, rollovers, or foreign accounts and assets.
Repeal or narrowing of the statutory CBDC bar, a retail CBDC pilot, or a digital euro holding cap cited by U.S. officials as a model.
The final outbound-investment rule widening to publicly traded securities, index funds, or more countries or technologies.
FinCEN section 9714 or 311 orders reaching widely used U.S. payment apps, stablecoins or exchanges that serve ordinary Americans, rather than offshore firms tied to sanctions evasion.
Any U.S. order limiting ordinary investors' ability to sell stocks or fund shares during a market slide, beyond exchanges' automatic circuit breakers and short-sale curbs.
A U.S. bill or rule that would ban or cap large cash payments, as Canada's Bill S-8 proposes, instead of only requiring businesses to report them.
A state law that caps or bans ordinary cash withdrawals, bank transfers or cash payments, going beyond limits on crypto ATMs.

H.R. 9331 or a similar bill passing the House or riding on a must-pass bill, or any rule making bank holds mandatory or letting banks or agencies hold whole classes of payments rather than specific suspected-fraud cases.
Officials proposing withdrawal delays, 'speed bumps' or caps on fast or automated (AI-driven) deposit outflows, rather than faster Fed lending to banks, in response to quicker bank runs.
Any U.S. proposal to cap stablecoin transfers or to require approval to convert dollars into stablecoins or send them abroad, as Thailand and Nigeria have done.
A final customer due diligence rule or guidance that requires banks to close or refuse accounts based on immigration status, rather than only allowing risk-based questions.
